subject: psychology
topic: A picture of eyes on the wall does not make people more generous
angle: While some meta-analyses show that eye cues reduce antisocial behavior, other meta-analyses suggest these cues do not influence donation amounts.
title: The illusion of surveillance

hooks.text: Does watching eyes make you a better person?
Eyes reduce bad behavior but do not increase donations.
You are being watched, but it is not changing your generosity.
A poster on a sterile white wall.

reveal.headline: Eyes on a wall do not make you more generous.
reveal.body: While eye cues reduce antisocial behavior, they do not influence how much you donate. The evidence is mixed.

explain.headline: The effect of surveillance is inconsistent.
explain.body: Research shows that stylized images of eyes can reduce antisocial behavior by 35%. However, these same cues do not change donation amounts in economic games.

matters.headline: Presence matters more than imagery.
matters.body: The number of people around you during a decision may be a more significant factor than the visual cues on the wall. This may be why your behavior feels unpredictable.

example.headline: The donation box in the lobby.
example.body: You walk past a jar for charity. A poster with eyes watches you. You decide whether or not to reach into your pocket.

question.headline: Who is actually watching your choices?

stat.label: reduction in antisocial behavior from photographs of eyes

claims.text: Two meta-analyses on the effect, which focused on generosity measured by donations and economic games, suggest that artificial surveillance cues do not influence the donation amount.
claims.quote: Two meta-analyses on the effect, which focused on generosity measured by donations and economic games, suggest that artificial surveillance cues do not influence the donation amount.

claims.text: Women give more than men in South America, North America and Oceania, while they give less than men in South Africa.
claims.quote: On the other hand, women give more than men in South America, North America and Oceania, while they give less than men in South Africa.

claims.text: A meta-analysis of 15 experiments involving 2035 participants shows that photographs and/or stylized images of eyes reduced antisocial behaviour by 35%.
claims.quote: Our meta-analysis of 15 experiments involving 2035 participants shows that photographs and/or stylized images of eyes reduced antisocial behaviour by 35%.

claims.text: Women are on average significantly more generous than men, even if controlling for several moderator variables that are included in the study.
claims.quote: It is found that gender differences exist, being women on average significantly more generous than men, even if controlling for several moderator variables that are included in the study.

verdict: The evidence is contradictory, showing that eye cues may reduce antisocial behavior but do not necessarily increase generosity in donation-based settings.
caveat: The number of people around when a donation decision is made is identified as a potentially important factor that can bias results.
caption:
Visual cues like eyes might change how you behave in public. 

Meta-analyses show that while these images can reduce antisocial behavior by 35%, they do not influence how much people donate. The presence of others may be a more important factor. 

How do you think your behavior changes when you feel observed?
